items.title: The Hidden Curriculum of Generative AI: Institutional AI Policies and the Potential for Student Inequality
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, prompting institutions to develop policies governing its use in teaching, learning, and assessment. Although existing discussions have emphasized academic integrity, assessment practices, and technological access, less attention has been given to the knowledge and competencies students may need to interpret and comply with institutional AI policies. This study examines how institutional GenAI policies establish explicit and implicit expectations for students and identifies potential pathways through which policy-navigation demands may contribute to educational inequality. Using comparative qualitative content analysis, publicly available policies and guidance documents from 20 purposively selected higher education institutions across the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia, and South Africa were examined. The analysis considered policy permissiveness, disclosure requirements, instructor discretion, student responsibilities, AI-literacy guidance, accessibility, equity, and implicit navigation demands. Findings indicate that acceptable AI use is frequently determined at the course, instructor, or assessment level, requiring students to interpret context-specific rules, understand disclosure requirements, verify AI-generated outputs, and reconcile varying instructor expectations. However, explicit consideration of differences in technological access, language, accessibility, and institutional knowledge was less consistently evident across the reviewed documents. items.title: The Human Factor in Access Control and Authentication: A Comprehensive Survey Analysis
items.abstract: In today's digitally-driven landscape, data security is paramount as organizations, governments, and individuals increasingly rely on interconnected systems to manage sensitive information. While technical aspects of access control and authentication mechanisms have been extensively studied, the human dimension remains under-explored. This research investigates user perceptions, adoption patterns, and security consciousness regarding traditional and emerging authentication mechanisms through a comprehensive survey of 450 participants across diverse demographics. The study reveals significant gaps between perceived security and actual usage patterns, with password-based systems maintaining dominance (4.6/5 usage frequency) despite low security perceptions (2.5/5). Multi-factor authentication (MFA) shows strong security perception (4.2/5) but moderate adoption (3.4/5), primarily influenced by organizational size and IT proficiency. Emerging technologies like AI-driven access control and blockchain authentication show promising adoption willingness (3.5/5) but face significant privacy (3.8/5) and complexity (3.5/5) concerns. The research identifies critical human factors affecting security implementation success and provides evidence-based recommendations for designing more effective, user-centric security systems that balance security requirements with usability considerations.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Mathematical Prestige: Epistemic Burden, Professional Identity, and Status Threat Under Automated Discovery
items.abstract: Automated mathematical discovery can increase the supply of results while changing the distribution of verification labour, research autonomy, and academic recognition. This theoretical working paper separates epistemic burden, professional identity, status threat, and governance concerns rather than treating opposition as evidence of jealousy. A small additive model distinguishes discovery-label-invariant formal validity from workload and utility. Eight Lean-checked propositions establish conditional workload relations, the possibility of overload, and the non-identification of latent motives from aggregate opposition. Public primary sources provide context but no representative psychological evidence. Deterministic synthetic examples illustrate the assumptions, and a prospective factorial study is proposed to test responses to source labels, verification packages, and credit rules. No participants were recruited and no empirical effects were estimated. The framework’s central contribution is an auditable separation of deductive consequences, documented positions, and hypotheses requiring evidence.

items.title: The impact of GenAI on the future of requirements engineering
items.abstract: Abstract Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), are transforming how we design and build systems by increasing access to domain knowledge and by providing automation support to software engineering (SE). As implementation becomes less expensive through generalist SE agents, engineering effort shifts away from writing correct code and toward expressing, curating, verifying, and evaluating requirements. In this paper, we survey the state of the art in AI for requirements engineering (RE) research leading up to the transformation, before reviewing advances in LLMs. We survey two subsequent research areas: prompt programming, which treats LLM instructions as a program in SE vernacular, and generalist SE agents, which combine multiple LLM advances to yield semi-autonomous processes that complete SE tasks. Finally, we explore the future of requirements engineering along two axes: matters changing how we interact with requirements through the SE process, and matters changing how requirements are experienced by software developers and stakeholders more broadly, including end-users. This article aims to inform how RE researchers can navigate this transformation in the selection of future research priorities.

items.title: The Impact of Imperfect XAI on Human-AI Decision-Making
items.abstract: Explainability techniques are rapidly being developed to improve human-AI decision-making across various cooperative work settings. Consequently, previous research has evaluated how decision-makers collaborate with imperfect AI by investigating appropriate reliance and task performance with the aim of designing more human-centered computer-supported collaborative tools. Several human-centered explainable AI (XAI) techniques have been proposed in hopes of improving decision-makers' collaboration with AI; however, these techniques are grounded in findings from previous studies that primarily focus on the impact of incorrect AI advice. Few studies acknowledge the possibility for the explanations to be incorrect even if the AI advice is correct. Thus, it is crucial to understand how imperfect XAI affects human-AI decision-making. In this work, we contribute a robust, mixed-methods user study with 136 participants to evaluate how incorrect explanations influence humans' decision-making behavior in a bird species identification task taking into account their level of expertise and an explanation's level of assertiveness. Our findings reveal the influence of imperfect XAI and humans' level of expertise on their reliance on AI and human-AI team performance. We also discuss how explanations can deceive decision-makers during human-AI collaboration. Hence, we shed light on the impacts of imperfect XAI in the field of computer-supported cooperative work and provide guidelines for designers of human-AI collaboration systems.

items.title: The indirect effect of artificial intelligence awareness on counterproductive work behavior: A meta-analytic study
items.abstract: BackgroundAs artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into the workplace, an important question concerns how employees respond when technological change is perceived as threatening rather than beneficial. Prior studies have examined several mechanisms linking AI awareness to employee attitudes and behaviors, but these mechanisms are often studied separately, limiting understanding of the broader psychological process underlying adverse employee reactions.ObjectiveThis study examines the mediating roles of job insecurity and psychological contract breach in the relationship between AI awareness and counterproductive work behavior (CWB).MethodsUsing meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM), we synthesized 45 independent studies involving 16,140 participants to test whether AI awareness influences CWB sequentially through job insecurity and psychological contract breach.ResultsBased on a pooled true-score correlation matrix, AI awareness was positively associated with job insecurity and CWB. Job insecurity was positively associated with psychological contract breach, which in turn was positively associated with CWB. The MASEM results indicated a significant but modest sequential indirect effect of AI awareness on CWB through job insecurity and psychological contract breach, alongside a substantial direct effect of AI awareness on CWB.ConclusionThe findings clarify how awareness of AI may contribute to negative workplace behavior. Job insecurity and psychological contract breach constitute a significant but relatively modest sequential pathway linking AI awareness to CWB. Because a substantial direct effect remained, additional psychological and organizational mechanisms are likely to contribute to employee responses to AI-related workplace change. These findings extend research on employee reactions to emerging workplace technologies.

items.title: The integration of artificial intelligence and Industry 4.0 in digital supply chains: A systematic review of e-commerce evolution under Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030
items.abstract: Background: Saudi Arabia prioritises adopting artificial intelligence (AI) and Industry 4.0 for e-commerce and digital supply chains under Vision 2030, but implementation and alignment with diversification goals remain insufficiently synthesised in the literature. Objectives: The study examines the impact of AI and automation on digital supply chains, identifies drivers and obstacles in Saudi Arabia’s e-commerce, and assesses their alignment with Vision 2030’s sustainability and diversification goals. Method: Following preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses, 30 peer-reviewed articles from 2020 to 2026 were reviewed from IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar, using bibliometric and thematic analysis. Results: Findings indicate that AI accounts for 46% of variability in sustainable performance; hybrid machine learning models reduce demand prediction error by 8.58% and achieve forecasting accuracy of up to 92%. Saudi Arabia’s 99% internet penetration supports Internet of Things development, but organisational barriers such as cultural resistance, cost, and job displacement (0.51) dominate adoption challenges over technical issues. Conclusion: Digitalisation success relies on technical and social systems, including government training and cybersecurity, to leverage AI for economic diversification beyond oil under Vision 2030. Contribution: The study connects national strategies to digital transformation, emphasising cybersecurity, workforce training, and the integration of technical and social systems, acknowledging immersive and decentralised tech as foundational for next-generation IoT and e-commerce.

items.title: The moderating role of tough love on relations between servant leadership and follower outcomes
items.abstract: Is servant leadership really a Disneyland-inspired fantasy of sunshine, lollipops, and hand-holding that makes followers complacent and lowers the bottom line of organizations, as critics claim? This criticism overlooks that servant leaders, striving to bring out the full potential in followers, do not only give positive strokes but may also provide followers with critical feedback. To assess the role of critical feedback in mitigating the flaws of servant leadership raised by critics, this study introduces tough love, the delivery of criticism with a positive tone and clear intent to help recipients overcome their deficiencies. We hypothesize that the relationship between servant leadership and key outcomes, such as follower performance, is strengthened the more servant leaders provide followers with tough love. We contend that tough love is appreciated by followers, solidifies relationships with their leaders, and helps them to grow through self-expansion. We reason that this growth benefits their work behaviors and attitudes. With multi-source field data covering three points in time, controlling for positive and negative feedback and prior levels of dependent variables, tough love is shown to moderate relations between servant leadership and both in-role performance and organizational citizenship behaviors, with mixed results for creativity and turnover intentions.

items.title: The Power of Storytelling in Film: Examining AI's Influence on Artistic Expression and Creative Processes
items.abstract: This paper explores the enduring power of storytelling in film and critically examines the transformative impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on creative processes within the film industry. Utilizing the Creative Cognition Framework and the Csikszentmihalyi’s Systems Model of Creativity, this study investigates how AI tools influence both generative and exploratory cognitive processes in film storytelling. A qualitative methodology, combining a comprehensive literature review with thematic analysis of questionnaire responses from 20 film and multimedia students at the University of Abuja, Nigeria, reveals nuanced insights. Findings indicate that AI significantly augments creative processes by enhancing efficiency, facilitating idea generation, and streamlining production tasks. However, respondents consistently emphasize AI's limitations in replicating human emotional depth, cultural understanding, and originality, advocating for a hybrid human-AI collaborative approach. The paper contributes to the understanding of human-AI collaboration in creative domains, highlighting opportunities for innovation while reaffirming the irreplaceable essence of human artistry in storytelling.

items.title: The Reasons Research and AI Thrive Together
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming scientific research by expanding investigators’ capacity to examine complex information, identify unrecognized relationships, generate hypotheses, and develop innovative solutions to scientific challenges. This article examines the relationship between human scientific expertise and artificial intelligence, emphasizing AI’s computational capabilities alongside the importance of human judgment, methodological rigor, and scientific accountability. Drawing upon peer-reviewed research involving molecular biology, materials science, pharmaceutical discovery, autonomous experimentation, and human–AI collaboration, the investigation demonstrates how computational intelligence can extend scientific inquiry beyond the limitations of conventional research methods. Attention is given to AI-assisted knowledge synthesis, interdisciplinary discovery, hypothesis generation, and the identification of solutions within multidimensional research environments. The article evaluates concerns regarding algorithmic bias, hallucinated information, intellectual originality, research integrity, and the reliability of computationally generated conclusions. It argues that the legitimacy of AI-assisted research should be determined by evidentiary accuracy, methodological transparency, reproducibility, and independent verification rather than the technological origins of research assistance. Ultimately, the article concludes that artificial intelligence does not diminish the intellectual authority or responsibility of human researchers but can amplify their investigative capabilities. The integration of human expertise and computational intelligence represents an emerging scientific paradigm capable of accelerating discovery, broadening research participation, and expanding the boundaries of human knowledge.

items.title: The unbearable (and unsustainable) social impact of AI-generated “cultural monism” and the EU digital legislation
items.abstract: The increasing use of generative AI (genAI) across cultural and (re)creative sectors is indisputable in contemporary times. Within the EU, these systems are classified as “general-purpose AI” models (Recital 99 of the Artificial Intelligence Act – AI Act) and are expected to deliver a wide range of economic and societal benefits, as affirmed in Recital 105 of the Act. Yet, significant concerns have emerged regarding their potential impact on individuals, civil society, and democracy. In the cultural domain, genAI technologies are widely employed to generate outputs often perceived as original. However, scholarly debate has increasingly highlighted the risk that their widespread diffusion may lead to a form of cultural impoverishment – understood as the depletion of cultural pluralism and diversity of artistic expression resulting from the pervasive use of these systems and their underlying architectures, as well as, ultimately, an increasing standardization of the outputs of the algorithmic creative process. These systematic risks are not merely social or political but also carry significant legal implications. The potential effects of genAI on freedom of (artistic) expression and cultural pluralism may, in fact, infringe upon fundamental rights enshrined in international human rights charters. Yet, the role of legal scholarship in addressing such risks remains uncertain. A promising conceptual instrument for tackling this issue is the notion of systemic risk, recently introduced in two key pieces of EU digital legislation: the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the mentioned AI Act. This article examines the advantages and limitations of employing this concept to address the risk of cultural impoverishment. The analysis focuses primarily on the EU legal framework, with particular attention to the AI Act, while adopting a functional and comparative perspective, given that the principal challenges stem from US-based AI systems. It also situates the inquiry within the broader dynamics of the data economy, specifically the logic of knowledge capitalism. The article begins by exploring the potential impacts of genAI on cultural pluralism and artistic expression, assessing whether these may with time culminate in cultural impoverishment – or even a transition toward cultural monism, marked by the predominance, in all the cultural productions, of a single mainstream culture. It then analyses whether EU digital regulation is equipped to subsume such phenomena within the legal category of systemic risk.

items.title: The Unnoticed Freezes in the AI Era
items.abstract: In 2023, 18% of American adults said they had ever used ChatGPT. By early 2026, that number was 44%. AI adoption in the workplace has been even more remarkable. According to Microsoft's 2024 Work Trend Index, 75% of knowledge workers were already using AI at work, with nearly half having started within the preceding six months. We did not vote to hand over drafting, summarizing, fact-checking, and even thinking to these systems. There was no big decision. Just a free chatbot, a looming deadline, and a prompt that saved twenty minutes. Then another, and another... Regarding this serious issue, I was drawn to a new paper quietly posted on SSRN last September by Professor Vuong Quan Hoang. It gives this slow handover a name: the Correction Freeze Problem (CFP). His question is simple: can a system think it is fine while it is drifting away from reality, and stay that way not because it is lazy or lying, but because the very way it corrects itself makes staying blind the rational choice? The paper answers yes. In four different ways. And when any of those ways meets a world that rewards going along, the drift becomes a trap that is much harder to escape than it was to fall into. To grasp these insights, you don't need the math. Simply because you've lived it.

items.title: Theoretical Approaches to Understanding Sustained Physical Activity Behaviour
items.abstract: Physical activity is an essential requirement for a healthy life. And physical activity should be sustained for a long term. While there is a broad understanding and agreement that it is needed, per WHO report (2022) nearly 50% of Indian adult population does not do the required physical activity. There can be several reasons including COVID impact, Work from Home, Digital service revolution, etc. contributing to this inactivity. While these factors have a negative impact on physical activity, individual (intrinsic) factors do have an impact on behaviour of physical activity. There are several theories relating to human behaviour. This paper focusses on what theories can be leveraged to enable people to develop sustained physical activity behaviour. Two important psychological theories – Self Determination Theory (SDT) and Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) are established theories in human behaviour domain. Components of these 2 theories and to what extent they relate to sustained physical activity behaviour are discussed in this paper. 25 participants of a physical activity program were interviewed. They were able to develop sustained physical activity. Researches in this area – SDT and TPB, empirical studies provide valuable insights into application of these theories to develop programs / interventions (by health care, government, fitness centres, families, peers, friends). Programs may need to be customized by agencies to enhance intrinsic motivation and behavioural intent that will have a positive impact on bringing the desirable change in individuals. Programs will need to apply other components of SDT and TPB as appropriate such that it contributes to the cause.

items.title: Think Faster, Argue Smarter: Combining GenAI-Assisted Prep and Human-Centered Rebuttals to Enhance Critical Thinking in Structured Debates
items.abstract: This experiential exercise adapts the traditional Oxford-style debate format to channel the pervasive student usage of Generative AI (GenAI) into a productive tension, inviting students to sharpen their critical reasoning, rhetorical discernment, and real-time argumentation skills. Students use GenAI to help them develop initial arguments and counterarguments, then engage in real-time rebuttals where they must think independently, respond to novel challenges, and adapt beyond their GenAI-prepared materials. This approach transforms GenAI from a potential crutch into a pedagogical catalyst that reveals the irreplaceable value of audience engagement, human judgment, critical thinking, and adaptive reasoning. The exercise forces students to scrutinize reasoning (both GenAI’s and their own) against standards of logic, clarity, and relevance, by confronting GenAI-assisted arguments and then dealing with spontaneous counterarguments. The exercise has been implemented in undergraduate strategic management and business ethics classes. It can also be valuable for higher-level courses and for other course subjects.

items.title: Toward “Obesityomics”: Domain‐Specific Omics in Precision Obesity Medicine with a Brief AI Perspective
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Obesity's global rise has outpaced the effectiveness of "one-size-fits-all" prevention and treatment strategies. The promise of precision medicine lies in addressing the etiological and biological diversity of obesity and transforming it into actionable endotypes. OBJECTIVES: In a narrative review, we analyze "obesityomics," looking at the contributions each omics layer makes to understanding and managing obesity. The areas we evaluate are genomics (heritability, polygenic risk, and monogenic forms), epigenomics (development and environment imprinting), transcriptomics (tissue-specific programs of adipose, liver, muscle, and hypothalamus), proteomics (signaling networks and adipokines), metabolomics and lipidomics (fuel partitioning, lipotoxicity, and metabolic inflection points), and microbiome science (metabolites, host-microbe interactions, and microbial ecology). Our domain-by-domain (single-omics) approach demonstrates how disease taxonomy, causal pathways, and biomarkers can be refined and targeted therapeutically. DISCUSSION: We argue that "obesityomics" is a pragmatic approach to aligning omics modalities to the right questions at the right time, not a wholesale merger of datasets. Artificial intelligence (AI)-including machine learning and deep learning-should be used in conjunction with quality control, feature selection, modest data integration, and obesity intervention prediction. Among the key challenges in managing sensitive multilayer data are harmonization, standardization, reproducibility, equitable representation, and governance. The translation priorities include prospective studies related to patient-centered outcomes, biomarker panels that are clinic-ready, interoperability standards, and cost-effectiveness evaluations. CONCLUSION: The review maps concrete steps to assist people with obesity in making better choices by identifying what each omics domain excels at and introducing a brief AI perspective.

items.abstract: Risk management is one of the fundamental components of a company's success, whatever its sector of activity. This paper reviews the work done in the field of risk management, both traditionally and by integrating Artificial Intelligence. It highlights the way in which risk management was solved in the traditional way, discussing methods and approaches and citing the limitations of traditional risk management. It also outlines research into the integration of Artificial Intelligence into risk management in the various phases of the risk management process. Based on the open literature published in the various journals in the field of risk management, the stages of the risk management process are the result of human judgment, which may identify risks or, for psychological or/and social reasons, may not, so human subjectivity influences the risk identification phase and all phases of the risk management process. To reduce this subjectivity and to reduce human contact in this phase, our article proposes a model based on Artificial Intelligence that attempts to identify risks and treat them in order to reduce or eliminate existing risks.

items.title: TradeGraph: Learning Global Semiconductor Market Dynamics from International Trade Networks using Hybrid Graph Neural Networks
items.abstract: The global semiconductor industry has become a strategic pillar of the digital economy and mainly supports the artificial intelligence technology, cloud computing, advanced manufacturing, and modern electronic devices. Forecasting international semiconductor trade flows is therefore essential for governments, researchers, and policymakers. In this paper, we propose TradeGraph, a hybrid Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture that combines Graph Attention Networks (GAT), Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) and GraphSAGE through an adaptive gated fusion mechanism for bilateral trade flow prediction. This research used the BACI international trade database. First, we analyze the structural evolution of the global semiconductor trade network and identify its major trading communities. Then, we develop a hybrid GNN model that we compare with three baseline GNN architectures under a temporal train-validation-test split, to predict the semiconductor trade flow. Experimental results demonstrate that TradeGraph achieves the best predictive performance and exhibits lower variability across multiple independent runs. Our results reveal that the global semiconductor market is characterized by a limited number of major trade blocs and suggest an increasing importance of Asian economies in the global semiconductor trade network over the study period. These findings demonstrate the potential of hybrid Graph Neural Networks for analyzing and forecasting complex international trade networks.

items.title: Transforming Agriculture through Emerging Technologies for Sustainable Productivity
items.abstract: The convergence of robotics and precision agriculture (PA) marks a transformative shift in modern farming practices aimed at enhancing productivity and ensuring long-term sustainability. This chapter explores the integration of advanced robotic systems into agricultural operations to address critical challenges such as labor shortages, resource inefficiency, and environmental degradation. It provides an in-depth analysis of various robotic applications, ranging from autonomous tractors, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) (drones), and robotic arms to artificial intelligence (AI)-driven monitoring systems that contribute to site-specific crop management, precision irrigation, pesticide application, and harvesting. The chapter emphasizes how robotics, when combined with sensor technologies, data analytics, and machine learning (ML), enables real-time decision-making and optimized farm management. Furthermore, it discusses the socio-economic and environmental benefits of adopting robotic solutions, along with the barriers to implementation and future research directions. By offering a comprehensive overview, this chapter aims to serve as a foundational reference for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers committed to the advancement of sustainable and high-efficiency agriculture through robotics.

items.title: Transforming Mathematics Teacher Education Through Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation: Extent of Utilization, Challenges, and Strategies in Colleges of Education, Gombe State
items.abstract: This study investigated the extent of utilization, challenges, and strategies for transforming mathematics teacher education through artificial intelligence (AI) and digital innovation in Colleges of Education in Gombe State, Nigeria. Anchored on the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, the study adopted a descriptive survey design involving 75 stakeholders (21 administrators and 54 mathematics lecturers) drawn by census sampling from Colleges of Education in Gombe State. Data were collected using a validated 30-item questionnaire (Cronbach alpha = 0.84) and analysed using mean, standard deviation, and independent-samples t-test at the 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed that AI and digital tools are utilized to a low extent overall in mathematics teacher education (cumulative mean = 2.70), with only dynamic geometry software and mobile learning applications utilized to a high extent. Ten challenges were affirmed as significant, most notably inadequate ICT infrastructure, high cost of digital devices and data, and lack of institutional policy on AI use (cumulative mean = 4.06), while resistance to change and data-privacy concerns were not strongly endorsed as major challenges. Nine strategies were identified as needed to enhance AI and digital integration, most notably reliable electricity and internet infrastructure and regular capacity-building training for lecturers (cumulative mean = 4.05). The t-test results showed no statistically significant difference between administrators' and lecturers' perceptions across extent of utilization (t = 1.05, p = 0.30), challenges (t = 0.55, p = 0.58), and strategies (t = 0.60, p = 0.55). items.title: Translation indeterminacy and the distributional fallacy
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly associated with the distributional hypothesis, according to which (1) semantic meaning is grounded in distributional patterns of linguistic context, and (2) knowledge of cross-linguistic distributional correspondences allows for successful translation. This paper rejects the first claim as a causal inversion: linguistic distributions reflect patterns arising from meaning-making practices rather than constituting their source. At the same time, it accepts the second claim, arguing that translation -human or machine - can succeed without requiring access to meaning or reference. Knowledge of interlingual distributional correspondence and their inferential organization may be sufficient for translation. The paper develops an ecological-enactivist perspective, according to which reference and meaning are grounded in agent-environment interaction and stabilized through action-grounded concepts, forms of world-involving cognition that current LLMs do not possess.

items.title: Translators’ Gains and Pains in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: This study aimed to provide a comprehensive systematic review of research published in peer-reviewed scientific journals in Arabic and English between 2022 and 2026 that investigated the impact of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Copilot, and others, on translation and translation education among professional translators, translation students, and faculty members. The study used the PRISMA 2020 framework for systematic search, screening, and documentation, and employed a thematic analysis approach based on the model developed by Braun and Clarke. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria to 24 initial records, the final analysis included 18 studies. The findings revealed that the most significant benefits of using generative AI tools included improved efficiency and productivity, reduced time to complete translation tasks, support for post-editing processes, improved certain translation quality indicators, and the promotion of self-directed learning and the development of professional competencies among translators and students. At the same time, the results identified several challenges, most notably terminological accuracy issues, difficulties handling cultural and idiomatic expressions and local dialects, risks associated with overreliance on intelligent systems, and ethical concerns involving privacy, transparency, and professional accountability. The review also showed that the impact of generative AI varies by text type, specialized domain, and the assessment tools used. In addition, it highlighted limited evidence available concerning the Arabic language, particularly in areas such as legal translation, idiomatic expressions, and local dialects. This study contributes an interpretive framework based on the concept of “Gains and Pains” to explain generative AI’s dual impact on translation and translation education. The findings conclude that generative AI does not fully replace human translators; rather, it serves as a supportive tool that reshapes translators’ professional roles toward reviewing, verifying, and evaluating outputs. Accordingly, the study recommends integrating generative AI tools into translator training programs within clear pedagogical and ethical frameworks. They should also include post-editing, critical thinking, and output-verification skills, and support further specialized applied research in the Arab context.

items.title: TrustGuard: A Risk-Aware Human Oversight Framework for Safe Autonomous AI Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents can perform increasingly consequential actions on behalf of users, creating a need for human oversight that is proportional to the potential risk of each action. This paper presents TrustGuard, a lightweight and interpretable risk-aware human oversight framework for AI agents. TrustGuard automatically evaluates proposed actions using five factors: privacy risk, financial risk, data modification risk, irreversibility risk, and external impact. Each factor is scored from zero to five, producing a total score from zero to twenty-five. Based on the score, actions are classified as Low, Medium, or High Risk and mapped to autonomous execution, user confirmation, or human approval. A prototype was implemented using Python and Streamlit to demonstrate the framework. The rule-based analyzer was calibrated using 120 development scenarios and subsequently evaluated on a held-out pilot set of 30 new scenarios. TrustGuard correctly classified 27 of the 30 test scenarios, achieving 90 percent accuracy. The results demonstrate the potential of transparent risk-based oversight while also identifying limitations in detecting some security-sensitive and privacy-sensitive actions.

items.title: Tumor antigens across cancer progression: from immune recognition and selection to precision cancer immunotherapy
items.abstract: Tumor antigens provide the molecular interface between malignant transformation and host immunity, but their biological significance is determined by more than their molecular existence. Antigen clonality, abundance, processing, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) presentation, dendritic-cell function, T-cell recognition, spatial immune organization, and the surrounding tumor microenvironment (TME) collectively determine whether an antigen becomes immunologically visible and therapeutically actionable. Across cancer progression, tumor-cell antigenic states and the TME undergo reciprocal selection: immune pressure can eliminate highly visible clones while favoring antigen-loss variants, HLA defects, immune exclusion, suppressive myeloid and stromal states, and treatment-resistant populations. Recent single-cell, spatial and three-dimensional imaging, as well as immunopeptidomic studies show that this evolution is heterogeneous across tumor regions and anatomical compartments rather than a uniform linear process. This review therefore advances an antigen-TME co-evolution framework linking primary tumors, lymphatic and nodal immune compartments, systemic dissemination, distant metastatic niches, therapy, minimal residual disease, and recurrence. It critically evaluates the strengths and limitations of the classical immunoediting model; compares melanoma, breast, colorectal, lung, prostate, sarcoma, and virus-associated cancers according to antigen source, clonality, presentation competence, immune architecture, and dominant therapeutic bottleneck; and examines clinical translation through checkpoint blockade, cellular therapy, vaccines, antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, immunopeptidomics, and computational antigen prediction. Particular attention is given to the gap between predicted peptide binding and verified presentation or immunogenicity, the need for longitudinal rather than single-biopsy profiling, and the requirement for prospective validation of artificial-intelligence models. The central conclusion is that tumor antigens become clinically meaningful only when antigenic state and microenvironmental context are assessed together, providing a more rigorous foundation for precision cancer immunotherapy.

items.title: Universities as Engines of AI Sovereignty
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping governance and economic systems worldwide, yet many countries in the Global South remain dependent on technologies, infrastructures, and governance models produced elsewhere. This dependency reflects deeper patterns of digital colonialism, including data extraction, reliance on foreign cloud systems, and limited capacity to shape AI on local terms. Grounded in African empirical evidence with broader application across the Global South, this paper argues that universities are critical but overlooked institutions in efforts to strengthen AI sovereignty. While governments, firms, and civil society face persistent capability gaps, universities hold mandates that position them to build research capacity, cultivate technical and governance expertise, and coordinate innovation ecosystems. Drawing on political economy and higher education scholarship, the paper develops the Capability–Alignment–Impact (CAI) Framework to explain how universities can contribute to autonomous AI development through three pathways: strengthening foundational knowledge; improving coordination across government, industry, and civil society; and translating expertise into societal impact. The paper concludes by outlining practical implications for policymakers, development agencies, and university leaders seeking to support sovereign AI ecosystems in the Global South.

items.title: USE OF GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR DESIGNING ROBOTIC MODELS USING ENGINEERING GRAPHICS
items.abstract: The article examines the possibilities of using generative artificial intelligence in teaching the discipline “Engineering and Computer Graphics” in the design of robotic models for the processing industry. The feasibility of integrating generative artificial intelligence models into the design process of robotic systems as a means of developing spatial thinking, graphic competence, design skills, and digital skills of agricultural university students is substantiated. It is established that modern generative systems (ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Claude, DALL·E, etc.) support all stages of educational design, from developing technical specifications and generating product concepts to creating drawings and three-dimensional models, visualizing designs, preparing technical documentation, and analyzing possible design solutions. A methodology for using generative artificial intelligence in the educational project “Design of a Robotic Manipulator” is proposed. The methodology is based on the principles of project-based learning, STEM education, the competency-based approach, and the use of CAD systems. A structural model for integrating generative artificial intelligence into the process of graphic training has been developed. It includes the stages of problem formulation, concept generation, sketch creation, three-dimensional modeling, preparation of design documentation, and expert evaluation of the finished product. It is demonstrated that the use of generative AI contributes to increasing students’ motivation, developing engineering thinking, fostering digital literacy, and reducing the time required for routine operations in the design of robotic models.

items.abstract: The article examines main aspects of artificial intelligence use in master's degree teaching of Linguistics and Pedagogical Education spheres. Artificial intelligence is currently being actively integrated into the educational process, transforming traditional formats into a more dynamic one: it quickly analyzes information, adapts materials on demand, systematizes and structures information, and personalizes educational content. In this article, the authors emphasize the competent training of future specialists/qualified personnel who will possess in-depth knowledge of the theory and methodology of teaching foreign languages, as well as skills in using innovative technological advances in professional teaching, and will be in demand in the future labor market. Based on the conducted research, the essence of using AI tools in the educational and linguistic environment is revealed, allowing for increased individualization and interactivity in the foreign language learning process. The modern education system is currently undergoing an active digital transformation, driven by the rapid development of information technology and artificial intelligence (AI). It was concluded that artificial intelligence can offer enormous potential for improving the quality of education, reducing the time and effort required by teachers, and facilitating the independent work of master's students. The obtained results allowed us to expand the scientific understanding of the use of AI in educational process and identify solutions for its application by higher education teachers in practical classes. The study materials will be useful for education and philology researchers and teachers improving the educational process.

items.title: Using large language models to probe the limits of atom-centered structural descriptors
items.abstract: Mapping an atomic structure to a compact set of geometric descriptors is an essential step in any machine-learning application to atomic-scale modeling. A powerful and widely used approach can be understood as a discretization of the histogram of pair distances, triangles, etc., which results in a hierarchy of symmetry-invariant atom-centered descriptors. Unfortunately, the lower rungs on this hierarchy (two, three, four-body clusters) were found to be incomplete, with symmetry-unrelated pairs of structures having exactly the same descriptors. However, all the "degeneracies" reported so far are resolved by considering larger clusters of neighbors to build the descriptors. We report examples of 3D structures that are indistinguishable even if one considers clusters of up to seven neighbors, and to arbitrary order when considering a practical level of discretization of the descriptors, discovered with the assistance of large language models. The key ingredients in their construction can be traced to results that have been known for decades in different communities: the model was able to find the references and recognize their significance for the problem at hand. We believe that this experiment exposes an extremely fruitful usage pattern for Artificial Intelligence in science: translating results between different communities and application domains, accelerating the process by which serendipitous discoveries in a field become breakthroughs in another.
